title: Remarks and Q&A at New York Fed conference
summary: A hawkish re-hardening at the margin, delivered at a NY Fed conference the day after the June minutes and two days after his Jul 7 Fox Business interview. The single dovish element he leaned on Jul 7 — an energy-led improvement in the near-term inflation path from a seeming Middle East resolution — has unwound: hostilities resumed (Trump says the deal is void), so the upside risk to energy and inflation is back, even as Williams keeps a benign baseline ('reasonable' that oil falls over 6–12 months). He calls inflation 'too high' and, most notably, elevates AI-investment-driven demand to his MAIN inflation concern, stating explicitly that a sustained AI demand-over-supply impulse is something 'you don't look through' — you position policy to offset it. He lays out a two-sided reaction function but spends his emphasis on the hike leg ('other scenarios where inflation is more persistent and stays higher, which would call for tighter monetary policy'), and gives a concrete data test: core PCE running 0.2%/month in H2-2026 is consistent with continued disinflation, higher than that signals persistence. He will not pre-commit on July 28-29 ('we haven't even started the analysis') and reaffirms data dependence unchanged. Net: still a data-dependent hold, but the near-term inflation-risk balance has tilted back up and the hike option is explicit — a modest hawkish step up from Jul 7, slightly above his late-June read. Balance-sheet remarks (reform should target financial-system resilience, not a reduction number) are not a policy-stance signal.

key_quotes.quote: If this creates a sustained impulse to demand relative to supply in the inflation … I do think that's the kind of situation where you don't look through this. You basically say you need to have a monetary policy positioned … to offset the inflationary impulse from that.
key_quotes.context: On AI-investment demand — now his main inflation concern; the clearest hawkish conditionality of the appearance and the key marginal shift vs Jul 7

key_quotes.quote: other scenarios where inflation is more persistent and stays higher, which would … call for tighter monetary policy. I think that's the right way to think about it.
key_quotes.context: His two-sided reaction function, with the emphasis on the tightening leg

key_quotes.quote: A rate of core PCE of two-tenths a month in the second half of this year, that would be consistent with my view of a disinflationary process that's continuing. If it's higher than that, that would be a sign of inflation a bit more persistent.
key_quotes.context: A concrete, quantified data test for the reaction function — 0.2% m/m core PCE is the disinflation threshold

key_quotes.quote: The markets still expect oil prices to come down over the next six to 12 months. I think that's a pretty reasonable baseline.
key_quotes.context: Energy baseline still benign despite the war flare-up — but this is no longer the active disinflationary tailwind it was on Jul 7; the risk is now two-sided/up

key_quotes.quote: We haven't even started the process of doing an analysis.
key_quotes.context: Declines to pre-commit on the July 28-29 decision; reaffirms data dependence ('I have not changed')
